title: Merge Profiles Sharing an Email
statement:
You get a list of user profiles. Each profile is a list of strings: the first is the person's name, the rest are email addresses.

Two profiles belong to the same person if they share at least one email. This is transitive: if profile A shares an email with B, and B shares one with C, then A, B and C are all one person, even if A and C have nothing in common directly. Profiles with the same name but no shared email are different people. Profiles that share an email always have the same name.

Merge the profiles and return one entry per person: the name, followed by all of that person's distinct emails in sorted (character code) order. The people may be returned in any order.

examples.why: The first and third profiles share ann@x.io, so they merge. The last Ann shares no email with them, so she stays a separate person despite the same name.
The first two share nothing directly, but the third links them. Merging only pairs that overlap directly, in one pass, would leave two people.
An email listed twice still appears once in the result.

constraints: Names are letters only; emails are valid addresses
hints: Think of each email as a node. What should connect two emails?
Every email in one profile belongs to the same person, so link each email to the first email of its profile. People are then the connected components of that graph.
Union-find over emails: union every email with the first email in its profile, then group emails by their root, sort each group and put the name in front.

explain.intuition:
Comparing profiles pairwise and merging when they overlap gets messy, because a merge can make two earlier non-overlapping groups overlap. Switch the point of view: make emails the nodes. Inside one profile, all emails belong together, so connect them. A person is then exactly a connected component, and transitivity is handled for free.

Union-find is the natural tool: for each profile, union every email with the first one. You do not even need a full chain of edges; linking each email to one shared anchor is enough to put them in the same set. Afterwards, group emails by their root and remember which name each root came from.
steps: For every profile, and every email in it, record the owner's name and union the email with the profile's first email.
After all unions, walk every distinct email and add it to the group of its root.
For each group, sort the emails and put the name in front.
pitfalls: Grouping by name. Two different people can share a name.
Merging in a single pass over the profiles, which misses links that only appear later, like the third profile in the second example.
Keeping duplicate emails, either from one profile listing an email twice or from two profiles of the same person.

complexity.time: O(E log E) for sorting, where E is the total number of emails; unions are nearly O(1)

solutions.title: Email graph and DFS
solutions.idea: Connect each email to the profile's first email, then collect each connected component with an explicit-stack DFS.

solutions.title: Union-find over emails
solutions.idea: Union every email with its profile's first email. Emails with the same root belong to one person.

followups: Profiles arrive one at a time from a stream. How do you keep the merged view up to date?
Also merge on phone numbers. Does anything change in the approach?
